questions.prompt: What does boundary value analysis test?

options.text: Values at and around the edges of a valid range
Only the middle of a valid range
The maximum load a system can take
The boundaries between microservices

questions.explanation: Off-by-one errors cluster at edges, so for a 1-100 field you test 0, 1, 100 and 101. Testing 50 exercises the same code path as any other middle value.

questions.prompt: What is equivalence partitioning?

options.text: Splitting the test suite across machines
Grouping inputs that should behave identically and testing one per group
Dividing testers evenly across features
Balancing unit and integration tests equally

questions.explanation: If every value from 1 to 100 follows the same path, one representative covers the partition. It is how you cut a combinatorial space to a practical number of cases.

questions.prompt: Why is a fixed sleep the wrong fix for a flaky UI test?

options.text: Sleeps are not supported in most frameworks
It makes the test fail on fast machines
It guesses at timing and still breaks on a slow run
It prevents screenshots from being captured

questions.explanation: A sleep hides the race rather than removing it, and slows every run. Waiting for the actual condition, such as an element becoming clickable, is both faster and reliable.

questions.prompt: What does the test pyramid recommend?

options.text: Mostly end-to-end tests, with few unit tests
An equal number of tests at every level
Manual testing at the base of the suite
Many fast unit tests, fewer integration, fewest end-to-end

questions.explanation: Unit tests are fast and pinpoint failures; end-to-end tests are slow and flaky but prove the system works. An inverted pyramid gives slow suites nobody trusts.

questions.prompt: What does 100% code coverage guarantee?

options.text: The code is free of bugs
Every line ran during the tests
Every input combination was tested
All requirements are covered

questions.explanation: Coverage shows execution, not correctness. A test that runs every line and asserts nothing scores 100%, and coverage says nothing about missing requirements.

questions.prompt: What is regression testing for?

options.text: Testing statistical regression models
Measuring performance decline over releases
Confirming a change has not broken existing behaviour
Reverting a release to a previous version

questions.explanation: New work frequently breaks something that used to work. A regression suite is the safety net that makes changing existing code affordable.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?

options.text: A stub returns canned data; a mock also asserts how it was called
A mock is always slower
A stub can only be used in unit tests
They are identical in every framework

questions.explanation: A stub supplies state so the code under test can run. A mock additionally verifies interactions, which couples the test to implementation and makes it more brittle.

questions.prompt: Why is a test that depends on another test's leftover data a problem?

options.text: It uses more disk space
It fails when run alone or in a different order
It cannot be written in most frameworks
It always runs slower

questions.explanation: Order dependence breaks parallel execution and makes failures irreproducible in isolation. Each test should set up and tear down its own state.

questions.prompt: In Selenium, why is an XPath like /html/body/div[3]/div[2]/span a poor locator?

options.text: XPath is not supported by modern browsers
It is slower than any other locator
It breaks on any change to page structure
It cannot locate nested elements

questions.explanation: An absolute path encodes the whole layout, so inserting one wrapper div breaks it. A stable test id or an accessible role survives visual restructuring.

questions.prompt: What is smoke testing?

options.text: Testing under maximum load
Exhaustively testing one feature
Testing without any documentation
A quick check that core paths work before deeper testing

questions.explanation: It answers whether the build is worth testing at all. If login fails, running a four-hour regression suite wastes the time of everyone waiting on it.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the Page Object Model in UI automation?

options.text: It runs tests against multiple browsers at once
It generates test data automatically
It centralises locators and page actions so a UI change touches one file
It records user sessions for replay

questions.explanation: Without it, a renamed button breaks fifty tests. With it, the page class changes once and every test that uses it keeps working.

questions.prompt: What does a severity rating on a bug describe, as opposed to priority?

options.text: How technically difficult the fix is
How badly it affects the system when it occurs
How soon it must be fixed
How many users reported it

questions.explanation: Severity is impact, priority is urgency, and they diverge: a crash in a rarely used admin screen is high severity but low priority, while a typo on the homepage is the reverse.

questions.prompt: Why should automated tests run in CI rather than only on a developer's machine?

options.text: CI machines are always faster
It is the only way to run tests in parallel
Local runs cannot produce reports
Every change is checked in a clean, consistent environment

questions.explanation: A clean environment catches missing dependencies and machine-specific assumptions, and running on every change means nobody can forget.

questions.prompt: What is exploratory testing?

options.text: Simultaneously learning the system, designing and running tests
Running tests without any goal
Testing only new features
Automated random input generation

questions.explanation: It is structured investigation guided by what the tester keeps finding, which is how bugs outside the written cases surface. It complements scripted testing rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: What makes a good bug report actionable?

options.text: A description of who is at fault
A proposed code fix
Steps to reproduce, expected and actual behaviour, and environment
A screenshot only

questions.explanation: A developer must be able to reproduce it and know what should have happened. 'Login is broken' costs a round trip that a clear report would have avoided.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of asserting on an exact timestamp in a test?

options.text: Timestamps cannot be compared in most languages
It makes the test non-deterministic and time-zone dependent
It slows the test down measurably
It requires a database connection

questions.explanation: The value changes every run and shifts with the machine's zone, so the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code. Inject a clock or assert on a range.

questions.prompt: What is load testing intended to reveal?

options.text: Whether the UI layout adapts to screen size
Whether the code follows style guidelines
How the system behaves under expected concurrent use
Whether all links on a page work

questions.explanation: Load testing measures behaviour at realistic concurrency. Stress testing goes further to find the breaking point and check that the system fails gracefully.

questions.prompt: Why is testing in production sometimes necessary despite good pre-release testing?

options.text: Staging environments are always broken
It is cheaper than maintaining a test environment
Production has no monitoring requirements
Real traffic, data and scale cannot be fully reproduced elsewhere

questions.explanation: Data volume, third-party behaviour and real usage patterns rarely exist in staging. Canaries and feature flags make it safe by limiting exposure.

questions.prompt: What is a test fixture?

options.text: The known state a test starts from
A report of the last test run
The assertion library being used
A permanently deployed test server

questions.explanation: A fixture sets up the data and dependencies a test needs so it starts from a known state and can be repeated with the same result.

questions.prompt: Why should a flaky test be quarantined or fixed rather than retried automatically?

options.text: Retrying uses too much CI time
Retries hide real intermittent bugs and erode trust in the suite
Most CI tools cannot retry tests
Retried tests always fail eventually

questions.explanation: A flake is often a genuine race that will hit users. Blanket retries make the suite green while teaching everyone to ignore failures.

questions.prompt: What does API testing cover that UI testing does not do well?

options.text: Visual layout correctness
Browser compatibility
Edge cases and error codes, quickly and reliably
Accessibility of controls

questions.explanation: The API layer lets you drive malformed input and error paths directly, far faster and less flakily than clicking through a UI that may not even expose them.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a traceability matrix?

options.text: Tracking which developer wrote each test
Recording how long each test takes
Mapping code coverage to files
Mapping requirements to the tests that verify them

questions.explanation: It makes gaps visible: a requirement with no linked test is untested, which a coverage percentage would never reveal.

questions.prompt: In BDD, what is the Given-When-Then structure for?

options.text: Ordering test execution in the suite
Describing context, action and expected outcome in shared language
Defining the three environments a build passes through
Grouping tests by severity

questions.explanation: It gives testers, developers and business stakeholders one readable format, which is where its value lies. Automating it is secondary to agreeing on the behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why is testing with production-like data volumes important?

options.text: Small datasets cannot be loaded into test databases
It is required for GDPR compliance
Queries that are fast on 100 rows can be unusable on a million
Large data makes tests more readable

questions.explanation: Missing indexes and N+1 queries are invisible at small scale. Realistic volume, with sensitive fields masked, is what exposes them before users do.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a test after the bug it caught is fixed?

options.text: It should be deleted, since the bug is gone
It should be kept so the bug cannot return unnoticed
It should be marked as skipped
It should be moved to manual testing

questions.explanation: A regression test for a real bug is among the most valuable in the suite, because that code path has already proven it can break.
